column2: Your childhood, your great valour and your inauspicious birth among us, thought about, immeasurable one, Krishna, give us doubt.
Becoming silent for a moment, somewhat angry with affection, Krishna, thus addressed by those cowherds, said, best of Brahmins:

Cowherds, if you feel no shame at connection with me, or if I am praiseworthy to you, what is the use of deliberation?
brahmapuran:189:11	If you have love for me, or if I am praiseworthy to you, then treat me with the honour due to a kinsman, as kin.
brahmapuran:189:12	I am neither god, Gandharva, Yaksha nor Danava; I have been born your kinsman; so think nothing otherwise of me.
Hearing Hari's words, the fortunate cowherds, bound to silence, went to Bala, when Krishna was angry with affection.
Krishna, seeing the clear sky, the moonlight of the autumn moon, the blooming water-lily bed perfuming the edges of the directions,
and the line of forest charming with garlands of crying bees, together with the gopis turned his mind to love.
With Rama he sang sweetly, very dear to women, that lotus-footed one, having taken a vow there regarding the name.
Hearing the lovely sound of song, the gopis then quickly left their houses and came where Madhusudana was.
One gopi sang slowly, following his steps; another, giving attention, remembered only him in mind.
One, saying "Krishna, Krishna," became shy; another, blind with love, shameless, went to his side.
Another, staying inside the house, seeing her elder outside, closed her eyes and meditated on Govinda, absorbed in him.
Surrounded by gopis, Govinda honoured the night, charming with the autumn moon, eager for the flavour of beginning the Rasa dance.
The gopis, in throngs, bodies given to Krishna's deeds, wandered in Vrindavana when Krishna had gone elsewhere.
Then the gopis wandered, longing to see Krishna; in Vrindavana at night, Brahmins, they saw Krishna's footprints.
Thus in his many kinds of deeds the gopis, agitated, roamed together in the lovely Vrindavana forest.
Then the gopis, turned back, hopeless of seeing Krishna, came to the Yamuna bank and sang of his deeds, Brahmins.
Then the gopis saw coming Krishna, protector of the three worlds, of untroubled action, with a blooming lotus face.
One, seeing Govinda coming, greatly delighted, her eyes wide, said "Krishna! Krishna! Krishna!"
One, looking at Hari with brows arched and forehead like a tablet, drank the lotus of his face with her bee-eyes.
One, seeing Govinda, closed her eyes and, meditating on his form alone, shone as if established in yoga.
Then Madhava appeased one with loving speech, one with glances and brow movements, and others with the touch of his hand.
With those gopis of pleased minds Hari of noble conduct delighted respectfully in the Rasa company.
Though bound in the Rasa circle, the gopis did not rise toward Krishna's side with a mind firm in one place.
Taking each gopi by the hand, Hari made the Rasa circle, their eyes closed at the touch of his hand.
Then the lovely dance began, with the sound of moving bangles, following in order the autumn songs of poetry.
Krishna sang of the autumn moon, the moon-lily bed of moonlight; the gopis sang one Krishna's name again and again.
One gopi, turned by fatigue, bangles moving and heated, gave her arm-creeper on the shoulder of Madhusudana's...
One gopi, her arms playful, embraced and kissed Madhusudana, skilled in pretext of song and praise.
Hari's arms, touching the gopis' cheeks, became thick with sweat-water for the sprouting of hair-bristling like crops.
Krishna sang the Rasa song as long as the sound was high; the gopis sang it twice over as long as they said "Well done, Krishna."
When he went they followed, when he turned they came face to face; the cowherd women served Hari in forward and reverse order.
Madhusudana then sported with the gopis; that one moment was like ten million years without him.
Though forbidden by fathers, husbands and brothers, the cowherd women, loving love, delighted Krishna at night.
He too, Madhusudana of immeasurable self, honouring their youth, sported with them in the nights, destroyer of foes.
In their husbands, in them, and in all beings, the Lord, whose form is the Self, abides pervading all.
As in all beings space, fire, earth, water, wind and the self are, so he abides pervading all.
Once, at midnight, while Janardana was absorbed in the Rasa, Arishta, maddened, came frightening the cow-pen.
In the shape of a water-bearing cloud, sharp-horned, eyes like the sun, tearing the earth greatly with the fall of his hoof-tips,
repeatedly licking his lips with his tongue grinding, his tail thrown up in fury, his shoulder-bond firm,
with a lofty hump, hard to pass by measure, his back and limbs smeared with dung and urine, a terror of the cows,
his neck hanging, facing forward, his face marked with tree-blows, that Daitya in the form of a bull, causing the cows' embryos to fall,
killing everyone by force, roaming the forests always; then seeing him of terrible eyes, afflicted with great fear,
the cowherds and cowherd women cried "Krishna, Krishna." Then Keshava gave a lion's roar and a slap on his arm.
Hearing that sound, he went to face Damodara, horn-tips lowered in front, eyes fixed on Krishna's belly.
The evil-souled Daitya in the form of a bull ran at him. Seeing the mighty Daitya bull coming, Krishna
did not move from his place, with the sport of a contemptuous smile; and Madhusudana seized him as he came near, like a crocodile.
He struck with his knee at the belly, immovable by the holding of the horns; having destroyed the pride and strength of him held by the two horns,
he pressed Arishta's neck like wet cloth, tore out one horn and struck him with that very horn.
The great Daitya died, vomiting blood from his mouth. When that Daitya was killed, the cowherds praised Janardana as the hosts of gods had praised Thousand-eyed (Indra) when Jambha was slain.

There two sons of Vasudeva, born as portions of Vishnu, have indeed been born for my destruction; wicked, they are growing.
brahmapuran:190:12	The great sacrifice of the bow will be on the fourteenth; you must bring those two there for a wrestling match.
brahmapuran:190:13	Wrestlers Chanura and Mushtika are skilled in wrestling, mine; let all the world see the fight with them.
brahmapuran:190:14	The elephant Kuvalayapida, driven by his great mahout, will kill those two sinful sons of Vasudeva, children.
brahmapuran:190:15	Having killed them, I shall kill Vasudeva and the evil-minded Nanda the cowherd, and my father and the evil-minded Ugrasena.
brahmapuran:190:16	Then I shall seize all the cattle-wealth and property of all the cowherds, evil ones wishing my death.
brahmapuran:190:17	Except you, lord of givers, these Yadavas are wicked to me; I shall strive in order to kill them.
brahmapuran:190:18	Then I shall rule this entire kingdom, free of thorns and without Yadavas, with your help; therefore, hero, go out of love for me.
brahmapuran:190:19	And as the cowherds quickly bring buffalo ghee and curd as presents, so you must speak to them accordingly.
Thus commanded, Akrura, a great devotee, Brahmins, was pleased, thinking "Tomorrow I shall see Krishna," and was in haste.
Saying "So be it" to the king, he quickly mounted a chariot and left Mathura city, fond of Madhu.
Keshi too, proud of strength, Kamsa's messenger, impelled, desiring Krishna's death, came to Vrindavana.
With the earth's surface wounded by his hooves, shaking the clouds by tossing his mane, again crossing the path of moon and sun, he came to the cowherds' edge.
At his neighing sound the cowherds, the Daitya's horse, and the gopis, agitated by fear, took refuge in Govinda.
Hearing their "Save, save!" Govinda, deep as the thunder of a water-bearing cloud, said:

Enough of fear, cowherds; why be afraid of Keshi? By you, of the cowherd class, the valour of heroes is lost.
brahmapuran:190:27	What use is this one of little substance, who helps by neighing, a wicked horse driven by Daitya force, prancing?
brahmapuran:190:28	Come, come, wicked one; I am Krishna, bearing the Pinaka like Shiva with Pushan; I shall make all your teeth fall from your mouth.
Having said so, Govinda went before Keshi; open-mouthed, the Daitya also rushed at him.
Making his arm coiled, Janardana then put it into the mouth of the wicked horse Keshi.
By Krishna's arm entering Keshi's mouth, his teeth were broken like pieces of white cloud.
Krishna's arm in Keshi's body grew, Brahmins, like a disease neglected by friends, for destruction.
With split lips, vomiting much frothy blood, the corners of his mouth wide, his bonds loosened, his eyes rolling,
he struck the ground with his feet, releasing dung and urine, his body wet with sweat, wearied and without effort.
That very terrible Asura with open mouth fell, split in two by Krishna's arm, like a tree by lightning.
With his two feet, back, tail-half, ear, eye and nose, the two halves of Keshi shone.
Having killed Keshi, Krishna, surrounded by delighted cowherds, stood right there, unwearied in body, at ease, laughing.
Then the cowherds and cowherd women, amazed at Keshi's death, praised the lotus-eyed one, charming with love.
The Brahmin Narada, standing among clouds, came in haste, his mind overflowing with joy at seeing Keshi killed:

Well done, well done, lord of the world, that you, Achyuta, have in sport slain this Keshi, giver of trouble to the dwellers in heaven.
brahmapuran:190:41	The good deeds you have done in this incarnation, Madhusudana, by them my mind is amazed; by this I am gratified.
brahmapuran:190:42	Even Shakra and the gods are afraid of this horse, Krishna, with his shaken mane, neighing, looking at the clouds.
brahmapuran:190:43	Since by you this wicked Keshi has been killed, Janardana, therefore you will be sung in the world by the name Keshava.
brahmapuran:190:44	May it be well with you; I shall go. In the battle with Kamsa I shall meet you again the day after tomorrow, slayer of Keshi.
brahmapuran:190:45	When Kamsa, son of Ugrasena, with his followers is felled, you, supporter of the earth, will be the remover of the earth's burden.
brahmapuran:190:46	There, Janardana, the battles of the kings of the earth, led by you, are to be seen by me in many ways.
brahmapuran:190:47	I shall go, Govinda; a great task of the gods has been done by you. Having been honoured by you, may it be well with you; I go.
When Narada had gone, Krishna, unamazed, with the cowherds entered Gokula, the one vessel for the gopis' eyes to drink.

He who, infinite, bears the earth standing on a peak, has descended for the world's purpose and will call me Akrura.
brahmapuran:191:13	Salutations again and again to him whose maya, made of father, kin, friend, brother and mother, this world is not able to lift up.
brahmapuran:191:14	Mortals cross this vast ignorance, this yoga-maya, when he is set in the heart; salutation to him, whose nature is knowledge.
brahmapuran:191:15	He who is called by sacrificers the Sacrifice-Person, Vasudeva, and Vishnu by the eternal knowers of Vedanta — to him I bow.
brahmapuran:191:16	In whom the world is held, established in his abode, being and non-being: may he come to gentleness toward me by his being.
brahmapuran:191:17	On remembering whom the vessel of all welfare is born, the best of Purushas, always I go for refuge to Hari.
Thus thinking of Vishnu, his mind bowed with devotion, Akrura reached Gokula when the sun was somewhat shining.
There he saw Krishna at the milking of the cows, in the midst of the calves, with a radiance like a blooming blue lotus petal,
with eyes like blooming lotus petals, a chest marked with the Shrivatsa, long arms, a long, high chest, a prominent nose,
bearing a lotus face, the seat of playful smile, with high red nails, firmly planted on the ground with his feet,
wearing two yellow garments, adorned with forest flowers, with hands like dense dark creepers, a white lotus as an ornament,
white as swan, moon and jasmine, wearing blue garments, Brahmins; and after him he saw Balabhadra, delight of the Yadus,
tall, with lofty arms, a blooming lotus face, surrounded by a garland of clouds, like another Kailasa mountain.
Seeing those two, the greatly wise Akrura, his lotus face blooming and all his limbs bristling, became so, Brahmins.

That he who is this supreme abode, this supreme state, Vasudeva, who stands in this twofold way —
brahmapuran:191:27	let there be fruition of my eyes at once on seeing the Supporter of the world, a loud laugh; may even this limb, by the Lord's grace, be the path of fruit through the contact of the given limb.
brahmapuran:191:28	Today, touching my lotus hand, he of infinite glorious form will make it so, by whose fingers' touch all sins are destroyed and men obtain the unsurpassed success.
brahmapuran:191:29	So the gods, prompted by the Ashvins, Rudra, Indra and Vasus, joyfully give boons; they who with the discus took away the eyes of the Daitya lord's women,
brahmapuran:191:30	in whom Bali, placing water with mind and speech, obtained pleasures staying on the earth's surface, and the lord of immortals Shakra obtained rule of the thirty and a full manvantara.
brahmapuran:191:31	Alas, lord, I, made by Kamsa's acceptance a vessel of faults though faultless, shame on the doer who is not given honour, since my mind has been cast out by the good.
brahmapuran:191:32	Of him whose nature is knowledge, the heap of all beings, from whom faults are removed, ever manifest, what in the world of all men is unknown to him who dwells in the heart?
brahmapuran:191:33	Therefore I, my body bowed with devotion, go to the Lord of the universe, the Lord of lords, the partial incarnation of Purushottama, Vishnu the unborn, without beginning, middle or end.
Then, in the clear dawn, the mighty Rama and Krishna were ready to go with Akrura to the city of Mathura.
Seeing it, the gopi people, in tears, bangles loosened on their arms, sighing, greatly pained, said to one another:

Having reached Mathura, how will Govinda come back to Gokula? He will drink with his ear the honey of the city women's sweet talk.
brahmapuran:192:15	How will his mind, having taken its place in the speeches of playful city women, go to the village cowherds and cowherd women?
brahmapuran:192:16	By Fate, taking the essence of the whole cow-pen, the heartless wicked one has struck the gopi women.
brahmapuran:192:17	The speech with smile full of feeling, the gait lovely with sport, and the side-long glance of city women are exceedingly so.
brahmapuran:192:18	This Hari is rustic; by their chains of coquetry, how will he by any means come back to your side?
brahmapuran:192:19	This Keshava goes to Mathura mounted on a chariot, deceived by the cruel and ruined Akrura.
brahmapuran:192:20	Does this cruel one not know that people are devoted in love, that he takes this imperishable delight Hari elsewhere from us?
brahmapuran:192:21	He goes with Rama, utterly pitiless; Govinda has mounted the chariot; let haste be made to stop him.
brahmapuran:192:22	What do you say in front of the elders? It is not fitting for us. What will the elders do to us, burnt by the fire of separation?
brahmapuran:192:23	Nanda and the other cowherds are ready to go; none makes an effort to turn Govinda back.
brahmapuran:192:24	Good morning today to the night of the women of Mathura, to whom Achyuta's lotus face becomes a feast for the bee-like eyes.
brahmapuran:192:25	Blessed are those on the road who, unhindered, will bear their bodies with bristling hair on seeing Krishna go from here.
brahmapuran:192:26	A great festival will today be for the eyes of the citizens of Mathura city, from seeing Govinda's face.
brahmapuran:192:27	What dream have those fortunate women seen of Adhokshaja, those with wide eyes who will see him unhindered?
brahmapuran:192:28	Ah, having shown this great treasure to the gopi folk, the Creator, merciless, has today torn out their eyes.
With love Hari goes to Vraja loosening toward us; our bangles too quickly slip from our hands.
Cruel-hearted Akrura quickly urges the horses; thus among suffering women, whom does pity not touch?
Alas, alas, Krishna! See the dust of the chariot-wheel high up; the dust by which Hari is removed far, even that dust is no longer seen.
Thus, looked at by the gopi folk with great heart, Keshava with Rama left the soil of Vraja.
Going by a chariot with swift horses, Rama, Akrura and Janardana reached the Yamuna bank at midday.
Then Akrura said to Krishna, "You two stay here while I perform my daily rite in the Kalindi's water."
Told "So be it," the greatly wise one, having bathed and sipped water, entered the Yamuna's water and meditated on the Supreme Brahman, Brahmins.
He saw Balabhadra, adorned with a garland of a thousand hoods, with limbs white as jasmine, eyes wide like opened lotus petals,
surrounded by great wind-eating Vasuki's child-serpents, praised, adorned with a fragrant forest garland,
wearing two dark garments, with lovely crest-ornament, with lovely earrings, intoxicated, staying in the depth of the water.
On his lap he saw one dark as a dense cloud, with long copper-red eyes, four-armed, noble-limbed, adorned with discus and other weapons,
wearing two yellow garments, adorned with a variegated garland, like a cloud variegated with Indra's bow and lightning,
with Shrivatsa on his chest, brilliant with lovely armlets and crown: he saw Krishna, of untroubled deeds, with a white lotus ornament,
meditated on in the mind by Sanandana and other sages, siddhas of yoga, faultless, their eyes fixed on the tips of their noses.
Akrura, recognising Bala and Krishna, was amazed and quickly thought, "How have they come here?"
As he wished to speak, Janardana stopped his speech. Then coming out of the water he returned to the chariot,
and there saw both Rama and Krishna seated on the chariot as before, in human forms.
Immersed again in the water, he saw them just the same, praised by Gandharvas, sages, Siddhas and great serpents.
Then knowing the truth, that lord of givers praised Achyuta, the Lord, whose nature is all knowledge:

Salutation again and again to the Supreme Self whose form is the subtle elements, of inconceivable greatness, all-pervading, of many forms and one nature.
brahmapuran:192:49	Salutation to you of the form of sound, to you become the inconceivable oblation; salutation to you of the form of knowledge, higher than Prakriti, lord.
brahmapuran:192:50	You are the self of beings, the self of the senses, and the self of Pradhana; you are the Self and the Supreme Self; you, one, stand fivefold.
